title: The Vedas and the Many Paths
bigQuestion: How can one tradition hold many gods, many paths and many texts, and still be recognized as one family?

story.title: Lamps on a West Ridge Windowsill
story.kicker: On one autumn night, a row of small clay lamps turns an ordinary Chicago apartment into a place of welcome.
paragraphs: It is a cold evening in late October, a few blocks from Devon Avenue on Chicago's North Side. The sari shops and sweet shops along the avenue have been busy all week. Inside a second-floor apartment, a sophomore named Priya is kneeling by the front window with a box of matches. Her grandmother hands her small clay lamps, one at a time. Each lamp is a shallow dish of oil with a cotton wick. Priya lights them and sets them in a row along the sill.

The lamps are diyas, and tonight is Diwali, the festival of lights. Her grandmother explains, as she does every year, that the lights welcome Lakshmi, the goddess of good fortune, into a clean and bright home. Then she tells the other story too: how Prince Rama came home to the city of Ayodhya after fourteen years in exile, and how the people lit lamps to guide him. Priya has heard both stories since she was small. She asks which one is the real reason for the lamps.

Her grandmother laughs. In her family's village in Gujarat, she says, people told it one way. Her friend from Tamil Nadu tells it another way. Her neighbor downstairs, a Jain family, lights lamps tonight for a different teacher altogether, and Sikh families in the suburbs celebrate their own festival on the same night. The lights mean all of these things at once, she says. That is not a problem to solve. That is how it works.

On the small shelf by the kitchen, there is a home shrine. It holds a brass image of Ganesha with his elephant head, a picture of Krishna playing a flute, and a small lamp that is lit every morning. Priya's father will say a short prayer there before the family eats sweets and the younger cousins run outside with sparklers. The apartment smells of ghee, incense and fried dough.

Priya's question is a good place to begin studying Hinduism. Many religions trace themselves to one founder or one book. Hinduism has neither. It is a large family of traditions that grew in South Asia over more than three thousand years. It holds many texts, many forms of worship and many ways of naming the divine. This chapter follows the threads that tie that family together.
story.think: Priya's grandmother says a festival can have several meanings at once. What does that suggest about how to study a tradition with no single founder or book?

lessons.title: One Name, Many Paths
lessons.mainIdea: Hinduism is not one organization with one founder; it is a family of related traditions that grew in South Asia over thousands of years.
reading: Ask a Hindu in Chicago, in Mumbai and in Bali to describe their religion, and you may hear three different answers. One may speak mostly of the god Vishnu. Another may center her life on the goddess Durga. A third may talk about meditation and the self, with little mention of any deity. Scholars therefore describe *Hinduism* as a family of traditions, not a single church. It has no founder, no single sacred book and no central authority that speaks for everyone.

The word itself came from outside. Ancient Persians used the name of the Sindhu, the Indus River, for the people who lived beyond it. Over centuries, Hindu became a label for the people and traditions of India. Many Hindus prefer an older name from their own texts: *Sanatana Dharma*, often translated as the eternal way or the eternal order. The name suggests a truth that was not invented at one moment but has always been there.

What holds the family together? Most Hindus share certain things. They honor the Vedas as sacred, even if few read them. They share ideas such as karma, rebirth and dharma. They worship in homes and temples through offerings called puja. And they tell the same great stories, such as the Ramayana and the Mahabharata. Within that shared frame, the variety is enormous, and adherents often see that variety as a strength.

Today there are about 1.2 billion Hindus, according to common estimates. Most live in India, where Hindus make up roughly four in five people, and in Nepal. Large communities also live in Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, Indonesia's island of Bali, Mauritius, the Caribbean, Britain and the United States. The Chicago area is home to many Hindu families, temples and cultural centers.

words.d: a family of related religious traditions that grew in South Asia, with no single founder, book or central authority
a name many Hindus use for their tradition, often translated as the eternal way or eternal order
a person who follows or belongs to a religious tradition

look.title: Where Hindus Live
look.cite: Rounded common estimates from national censuses and research surveys; figures vary by source.
look.prompt: About what share of the world's roughly 1.2 billion Hindus live in India? What does that suggest about the tradition's geography?

check.q: Why do scholars describe Hinduism as a family of traditions?
choices: Because it was founded by a family of priests
Because it has no single founder, book or central authority, and its practices vary widely
Because every Hindu worships the same single deity in the same way
Because it is practiced only within families and never in temples
check.why: The reading explains that Hinduism has no founder, no single book and no central authority, so it is a family of related traditions.

check.q: Where does the word Hindu come from?
choices: A Sanskrit word for temple
The name of the first Hindu teacher
The Sindhu, or Indus, River, a name Persians used for the people beyond it
A British word meaning eastern
check.why: The name comes from the Sindhu (Indus) River, which ancient Persians used for the people who lived beyond it.

check.q: What does Sanatana Dharma, a name many Hindus prefer, usually mean?
choices: The eternal way or eternal order
The religion of the river
The book of the four Vedas
The festival of lights
check.why: Sanatana Dharma is often translated as the eternal way, suggesting a truth that has always existed.

lessons.title: The Vedas: Heard and Remembered
lessons.mainIdea: The Vedas are the oldest Hindu scriptures, hymns and rituals in Sanskrit that were memorized and passed down by mouth for centuries before they were written.
reading: Picture a boy in a traditional school in South India, sitting cross-legged in front of his teacher. The teacher chants a line in Sanskrit, and the boy repeats it exactly, with the same rise and fall of pitch. They do this for hours a day, for years. This is how the *Vedas* have been kept alive. For many centuries they were not written at all. They were memorized and chanted, with methods so careful that scholars think the wording changed very little.

The word Veda means knowledge. There are four Vedas: the Rig Veda, the Sama Veda, the Yajur Veda and the Atharva Veda. The oldest, the Rig Veda, holds more than a thousand hymns. Scholars date its earliest parts to roughly 1500 to 1200 BCE, though estimates vary. Many hymns praise deities of nature and ritual, such as Agni, the god of fire, and Indra, a god of storm and war. Priests chanted them at fire sacrifices.

Hindus divide their sacred texts into two kinds. The word *shruti* means what is heard. It refers to the Vedas, which many Hindus believe ancient seers heard or perceived rather than composed. The word *smriti* means what is remembered. It includes later texts written by human authors, such as the great epics, the law books and the Puranas. For many Hindus, shruti carries the highest authority, even though smriti texts are far more widely read.

Few Hindus today read the Vedas cover to cover. Yet Vedic verses are still chanted at weddings, at the thread ceremony that marks a boy's entry into study in some families, and at funerals. One famous verse, the Gayatri mantra from the Rig Veda, is recited daily by many Hindus as a prayer for light and understanding.

words.d: the four oldest Hindu scriptures, collections of hymns, chants and ritual texts in Sanskrit
the ancient classical language of India in which the Vedas and many other Hindu texts are written
what is heard; the Vedas, which many Hindus regard as revealed to ancient seers
what is remembered; later sacred texts with human authors, such as the epics and law books

look.title: Layers of Early Hindu Scripture
rows: Great epics begin to take shape
look.cite: Common scholarly estimates; dates for these oral texts are uncertain and debated.
look.prompt: Roughly how many centuries passed between the earliest Rig Veda hymns and the early Upanishads? Why are these dates so uncertain?

check.q: How were the Vedas passed down for many centuries?
choices: They were carved on temple walls
They were copied by monks onto paper scrolls
They were printed in books for every household
They were memorized and chanted from teacher to student
check.why: The reading explains that the Vedas were kept alive orally, memorized and chanted with great precision.

check.q: What is the difference between shruti and smriti?
choices: Shruti are prayers; smriti are hymns to Agni
Shruti is what is heard, like the Vedas; smriti is what is remembered, like the epics
Shruti is written in Sanskrit; smriti is written in English
Shruti is for priests only; smriti is only for children
check.why: Shruti means heard and refers to the Vedas; smriti means remembered and includes later texts such as the epics.

check.q: Which of these is one of the four Vedas?
choices: The Ramayana
The Bhagavad Gita
The Sama Veda
The Puranas
check.why: The four Vedas are the Rig, Sama, Yajur and Atharva Vedas. The Ramayana, Gita and Puranas are later smriti texts.

lessons.title: The Upanishads: Brahman and Atman
lessons.mainIdea: The Upanishads teach that behind the changing world is one ultimate reality, Brahman, and that the deepest self, atman, is one with it.
reading: The *Upanishads* are later texts attached to the Vedas, many composed around 800 to 300 BCE. Their name suggests sitting down near a teacher. Many are dialogues, in which a student questions a teacher about the deepest things: What is real? What am I? What remains when everything changes? Because they come at the end of the Vedas, they are also called Vedanta, the end or goal of the Veda.

One famous scene appears in the Chandogya Upanishad. A father, Uddalaka, tells his son Shvetaketu to drop salt into a cup of water and come back the next morning. The salt has vanished from sight, but every sip tastes salty. So it is, the father says, with the subtle essence of the world. You cannot see it, yet it is in everything. Then he adds the line that later teachers made famous: you are that.

That essence is *Brahman*, the one ultimate reality behind all things. The self at the core of each person is called *atman*. The Upanishads teach that atman is not the body, the thoughts or the personality, which all change. Many passages hold that atman and Brahman are, at bottom, the same. To realize this truth is to be freed from ignorance.

Hindu thinkers have read these texts in different ways. The teacher Shankara, around the 8th century CE, taught Advaita, or non-dualism: atman and Brahman are one, and separateness is an illusion. Later teachers such as Ramanuja held that the soul is real and distinct but depends wholly on a personal God. Both schools claim the Upanishads as their source.

words.d: philosophical texts at the end of the Vedas, often dialogues about ultimate reality and the self
in Hindu thought, the one ultimate reality that underlies and pervades everything
the deepest, unchanging self in each being; the Upanishads teach that it is one with Brahman

look.title: Salt in the Water
look.text: Place this salt in water and come to me in the morning. The son did so. The father said: bring me the salt you put in the water. The son looked but could not find it, for it had dissolved. Taste the water from the top, the middle and the bottom. It is salty. In the same way, my son, you do not see the true essence here, yet it is here. That subtle essence is the self of all that exists. It is the true. It is the self. And you, Shvetaketu, are that.
look.prompt: What is the salt meant to stand for? What claim is the father making about his son?

check.q: In the salt-and-water story, what does the dissolved salt stand for?
choices: An essence that cannot be seen but is present in everything
The ocean that surrounds India
The sweat of hard work
The food offered at a temple
check.why: In the Chandogya Upanishad, the salt is invisible but tastes in every sip, like the subtle essence that pervades the world.

check.q: What do the Upanishads mean by atman?
choices: The god of fire in the Rig Veda
A priest who chants at sacrifices
The deepest, unchanging self in each being
The cycle of birth and death
check.why: Atman is the true self. Agni is the fire god, and samsara is the cycle of rebirth.

check.q: How did Shankara and Ramanuja read the Upanishads differently?
choices: Shankara rejected the Upanishads; Ramanuja accepted them
Shankara taught that atman and Brahman are one; Ramanuja taught that the soul is real and depends on a personal God
Shankara wrote in Tamil; Ramanuja wrote in English
They agreed completely on every point
check.why: Shankara's Advaita holds atman and Brahman are one; Ramanuja held the soul is distinct yet wholly dependent on God. Both used the Upanishads.

sections.title: The Wheel and the Way Out

lessons.title: Samsara and Karma
lessons.mainIdea: Many Hindus believe the soul is reborn again and again in samsara, and that karma, the result of one's actions, shapes each new life.
reading: At a Hindu funeral, the body is usually cremated, and the family may later scatter the ashes in a river, ideally the Ganges. Mourners often say that the soul has moved on, not that it has ended. Many Hindus believe the atman sheds a body the way a person sheds worn-out clothes, then takes a new one. This round of birth, death and rebirth is called *samsara*, which means wandering or flowing on.

What decides the next life? The answer is *karma*. The word means action, and it also means the result that action brings. In the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, a teacher says that as a person acts, so that person becomes: good actions make one good, harmful actions make one harmful. Karma is not seen as reward and punishment handed out by a judge. Many Hindus describe it more like a law of nature, the way a seed grows into its own kind of plant.

Karma includes thoughts and intentions, not only deeds. It can shape the circumstances of a future life, and many believe it also shapes character in this life. Hindus do not all agree on every detail. Some stress that a gracious God can soften or remove karma. Others stress personal effort. But most agree that each person's choices matter, because they carry forward.

Samsara is not usually seen as a happy endless adventure. Even good rebirths end in death and more rebirth. For that reason, many Hindu texts describe samsara as something to be escaped. The next two lessons explain the ideas of right living and final release that answer this problem. Together, samsara, karma, dharma and moksha form a framework most Hindus share.

words.d: the ongoing cycle of birth, death and rebirth, from a word meaning wandering or flowing on
action and its results; the principle that one's deeds and intentions shape one's future, including future lives
the belief that the soul is born again in a new body after death

look.title: As One Acts, So One Becomes
look.text: As a person acts and as a person behaves, so that person becomes. One who does good becomes good; one who does harm becomes harmful. A person is made of desire. As the desire is, so is the will. As the will is, so is the deed. And whatever deed a person does, that the person becomes.
look.prompt: According to this passage, where does karma begin: with actions, or with something before actions? Trace the chain the text describes.

check.q: What does samsara mean in Hindu thought?
choices: The right duty of each person
The final release from rebirth
A festival of lights
The cycle of birth, death and rebirth
check.why: Samsara, meaning wandering or flowing on, is the cycle of rebirth. Dharma is duty and moksha is release.

check.q: According to the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad passage, how does a person's future take shape?
choices: As a person acts, so that person becomes
By the position of the stars at birth
By a judge who reads a list of sins
By chance, with no connection to one's choices
check.why: The passage teaches that one becomes what one does, and that deeds begin with desire and will.

check.q: Why do many Hindu texts describe samsara as something to escape?
choices: Because rebirth happens only once
Because even good rebirths end in death and more rebirth
Because karma applies only to priests
Because samsara forbids worship
check.why: Even a good life ends in death and further rebirth, so many texts look for release from the whole cycle.

lessons.title: Dharma: Duty and Right Order
lessons.mainIdea: Dharma is the right way of living, the duty and moral order that fit a person's role, stage of life and community.
reading: A young woman in Chicago must decide whether to take a job across the country or stay near her aging parents. A Hindu grandmother might ask her a question: what is your *dharma* here? Dharma is one of the richest words in Hindu thought. It can mean duty, law, right conduct, religion and the order that holds the world together. In daily life, it usually means doing what is right for your role and situation.

Classical Hindu texts teach that dharma is not the same for everyone. A parent, a student, a ruler and a teacher each have different duties. Some texts also describe four stages of life, called ashramas: student, householder, forest dweller, who steps back from worldly life, and renunciant, who gives up possessions to seek release. Few Hindus today follow all four stages strictly, but the ideal of life as a journey with changing duties remains.

The same texts name four goals of life, the *purusharthas*. Dharma is right living. Artha is prosperity and success. Kama is pleasure, love and beauty. Moksha is final release from rebirth. The first three are seen as good when they are pursued within dharma. Wealth and love are not condemned, but they are meant to serve a well-ordered life.

Hindus also speak of general duties that apply to everyone, such as truthfulness, self-control and *ahimsa*, not harming living beings. Many Hindus are vegetarian partly because of ahimsa. When personal duty and general duty seem to clash, the question becomes hard. That is exactly the problem Arjuna faces in the Bhagavad Gita, as the next chapter shows.

words.d: duty, right conduct and moral order; the right way to live for one's role and stage of life
the four goals of life in classical Hindu teaching: dharma, artha, kama and moksha
not harming living beings; a value shared by Hindus, Jains and Buddhists

look.title: Two Duties at Once
look.text: Ravi is a nurse and the oldest son in his family. During a winter storm, his hospital asks every nurse to stay for a double shift. The same night, his father calls: the furnace has broken and his mother is ill. Ravi has a duty as a nurse and a duty as a son. Both are part of his dharma.
look.prompt: Using the ideas of personal duty and general duty such as ahimsa, explain how Ravi might reason through his choice. Why does dharma not give one simple rule?

check.q: Which of these best describes dharma?
choices: A festival held in the spring
The deepest self in each person
Right conduct and duty that fit one's role and stage of life
Pleasure, love and beauty
check.why: Dharma means duty, right conduct and moral order. Atman is the self, and kama is pleasure and love.

check.q: Which list names the four goals of life, the purusharthas?
choices: Dharma, artha, kama, moksha
Brahman, atman, karma, samsara
Student, householder, forest dweller, renunciant
Rig, Sama, Yajur, Atharva
check.why: The purusharthas are dharma, artha, kama and moksha. The third choice lists the four stages of life, and the fourth lists the Vedas.

check.q: What role does ahimsa play in many Hindus' lives?
choices: It requires people to fast every Friday
It leads many Hindus to be vegetarian, out of a duty not to harm living beings
It tells people to worship only Shiva
It forbids people from working for money
check.why: Ahimsa means not harming living beings, and it is one reason many Hindus avoid eating meat.

lessons.title: Moksha: Release from the Wheel
lessons.mainIdea: Moksha is the final goal in much Hindu thought: freedom from the cycle of rebirth, understood in different ways by different schools.
reading: In the holy city of Varanasi, on the Ganges River, cremation fires burn day and night on stone steps called ghats. Many elderly Hindus travel there hoping to die in the city, because tradition holds that dying in Varanasi brings release. That release has a name: *moksha*, freedom from samsara. Moksha means liberation. It is the fourth and highest of the four goals of life.

What is moksha like? Hindu schools answer differently. In the Advaita tradition, moksha is the realization that atman and Brahman were always one, like a drop of water returning to the sea. In devotional traditions, moksha is often pictured as eternal loving closeness to a personal God, such as Vishnu or Shiva, while the soul remains itself. Both agree that moksha ends rebirth and suffering.

How does one reach moksha? Again, Hindus describe several ways, which later lessons call paths or yogas. Some stress knowledge and insight. Some stress devotion and the grace of God. Some stress selfless action. Some stress meditation. Many Hindus combine them. Most also believe that moksha may take many lifetimes, which is why living well now still matters.

Not every Hindu thinks about moksha daily. Many focus on good karma, family duty, worship and a good rebirth. Scholars sometimes note that the tradition holds both goals side by side: living well within the world, and seeking release from it. Each family and teacher balances the two in its own way.

words.d: liberation; the final release of the soul from the cycle of rebirth
a flight of stone steps leading down to a river, used for bathing, worship and cremation
being set free; in Hindu thought, freedom from samsara

look.title: Two Pictures of Release
look.text: Picture A: a drop of rain falls into the ocean. It does not disappear, but it is no longer a separate drop; it is the ocean. Picture B: a child runs home at the end of a long day and is held by a parent who has been waiting. The child is still the child, but now fully at home.
look.prompt: Which picture fits the Advaita view of moksha, and which fits a devotional view? What does each picture say about whether the self remains distinct?

check.q: What is moksha?
choices: A river in northern India
A reward of wealth in the next life
The first stage of life, as a student
Liberation from the cycle of rebirth
check.why: Moksha is liberation from samsara. Artha, not moksha, is the goal of prosperity.

check.q: Why do many elderly Hindus travel to Varanasi?
choices: To attend school at the city's temples
Because tradition holds that dying there brings release from rebirth
To celebrate Holi with colored powder
Because the Vedas were first written there
check.why: Varanasi is a holy city on the Ganges, and tradition holds that dying there brings moksha.

check.q: How do Advaita and devotional traditions picture moksha differently?
choices: Advaita sees it as realizing oneness with Brahman; devotional traditions see it as loving closeness to a personal God
Advaita denies moksha exists; devotional traditions accept it
Advaita says it comes after one life; devotional traditions say it never comes
They picture it the same way
check.why: Advaita holds that atman and Brahman are one, while devotional schools picture the soul close to God yet still itself.

lessons.title: Vishnu and His Avatars
lessons.mainIdea: Vishnu, the preserver, is worshiped by many Hindus as the supreme God who descends to earth in forms called avatars, including Rama and Krishna.
reading: In a Hindu temple in Aurora, west of Chicago, the central image shows a standing, dark-skinned figure crowned with gold. He is Venkateswara, a form of *Vishnu* widely worshiped in South India. Devotees line up to see him, a moment of worship called *darshan*, seeing and being seen by the deity. Worshipers of Vishnu are called Vaishnavas, and they form one of the largest groups of Hindus.

Hindu texts often describe three great functions of the divine: Brahma creates, Vishnu preserves and Shiva destroys so that renewal can come. Scholars call this grouping the Trimurti. In practice, few Hindus worship Brahma, and many see either Vishnu or Shiva as the supreme God who performs all three roles.

Vaishnavas believe that when goodness weakens and evil grows, Vishnu descends to earth to restore order. Each descent is an *avatar*. Tradition often lists ten, including a fish, a boar and a man-lion. The two most beloved are Rama, the ideal king of the Ramayana, and Krishna, the divine teacher of the Bhagavad Gita and the playful cowherd of many stories.

Many Hindus see no contradiction in honoring several deities. A common teaching, drawn from a Rig Veda verse, holds that truth is one, though the wise call it by many names. Some Hindus understand the deities as many faces of one divine reality. Others worship one supreme God and see the other deities as powerful beings under that God.

words.d: the Hindu god of preservation, worshiped by Vaishnavas as the supreme God
a descent; a form in which a deity, especially Vishnu, comes to earth
seeing and being seen by a deity, as when worshipers view a temple image
the grouping of Brahma the creator, Vishnu the preserver and Shiva the destroyer

look.title: Why the Divine Comes Down
look.text: Whenever right order declines and wrongdoing rises, I send myself forth. To protect the good, to end the work of evildoers, and to set dharma firmly in place again, I come into being age after age.
look.prompt: How does this passage explain the idea of avatars? What three purposes does Krishna name?

check.q: What is an avatar in Vaishnava belief?
choices: A priest who leads temple worship
A form in which Vishnu descends to earth to restore order
A clay lamp lit at Diwali
A stage of life for older people
check.why: An avatar is a descent of Vishnu to earth, as the Gita describes in 4.7–8.

check.q: Which two avatars of Vishnu are most widely loved?
choices: Ganesha and Hanuman
Brahma and Shiva
Agni and Indra
Rama and Krishna
check.why: Rama, hero of the Ramayana, and Krishna, teacher of the Gita, are Vishnu's most beloved avatars.

check.q: What does darshan mean?
choices: Seeing and being seen by the deity during worship
A song from the Sama Veda
A fast before a festival
A vow of silence
check.why: Darshan is the act of seeing the deity, and being seen, as when devotees view a temple image.

lessons.title: Shiva, Devi and Ganesha
lessons.mainIdea: Many Hindus worship Shiva or the Goddess, Devi, as supreme, and nearly all honor Ganesha as the remover of obstacles.
reading: A famous bronze sculpture from South India shows *Shiva* dancing inside a ring of flames. One foot stands on a small figure representing ignorance. One hand holds a drum, the sound of creation. Another holds fire, the force of destruction. Shiva's worshipers, called Shaivas, see him as the supreme God who creates, preserves and destroys in an endless cosmic dance. He is also pictured as a great yogi meditating on a mountain.

Other Hindus center their worship on the Goddess, often called *Devi* or Shakti, meaning divine power. Her followers are called Shaktas. She takes many forms. Durga rides a lion and defeats a buffalo demon. Kali, dark and fierce, destroys evil and ego. Lakshmi brings good fortune, and Saraswati brings learning and music. For Shaktas, the Goddess is the supreme power behind the universe.

*Ganesha*, with his elephant head, is honored by nearly all Hindus, whatever deity they worship most. In one well-known story, he is the son of Shiva and the goddess Parvati. He is called the remover of obstacles, so many Hindus pray to him before starting anything new: a trip, an exam, a wedding or a business. His image often stands near the doorway of homes and temples.

These traditions overlap. A family may keep images of Ganesha, Krishna and Durga on the same shelf. Some Hindus, called Smartas, worship several deities as equal forms of the one Brahman. The tradition makes room for devotion to one chosen deity while respecting others.

words.d: a major Hindu god, worshiped by Shaivas as supreme; often shown as a dancer or a meditating yogi
the Goddess; the divine as feminine, worshiped in forms such as Durga, Kali and Lakshmi
the elephant-headed Hindu god honored as the remover of obstacles

look.title: Reading a Sculpture
look.text: Shiva as Lord of the Dance: four arms; in one hand a small drum; in another, a flame; a third hand raised, palm out, in a gesture that means do not fear; the fourth pointing to his lifted foot. His other foot presses down on a small figure. A circle of fire surrounds him.
look.prompt: Using the reading, explain what at least three details in this sculpture might mean to a Shaiva worshiper.

check.q: Why do many Hindus pray to Ganesha before starting something new?
choices: He is the god of fire in the Vedas
He wrote the Upanishads
He is honored as the remover of obstacles
He rules the underworld
check.why: Ganesha is honored as the remover of obstacles, so Hindus call on him at beginnings.

check.q: Which statement about Devi is accurate?
choices: She is worshiped only in Bali
She is the Goddess, worshiped in forms such as Durga, Kali and Lakshmi
She is an avatar of Ganesha
She is a human teacher from the 8th century
check.why: Devi, or Shakti, is the Goddess, and Shaktas worship her in many forms.

check.q: What group of Hindus sees Shiva as the supreme God?
choices: Vaishnavas
Shaktas
Smartas
Shaivas
check.why: Shaivas worship Shiva as supreme. Vaishnavas center on Vishnu and Shaktas on the Goddess.

lessons.title: Four Paths to the Goal
lessons.mainIdea: Hindu teachers describe several paths, or yogas, toward moksha: knowledge, devotion, selfless action and meditation.
reading: Four people might all be walking toward the same goal. One sits with a teacher, studying the Upanishads and asking who she truly is. One sings devotional songs to Krishna every evening. One runs a free clinic and tries to work without seeking praise. One wakes before dawn to sit still and quiet the mind. Hindu tradition would say all four are practicing *yoga*, a word that means joining or discipline.

The path of knowledge is *jnana yoga*. It uses study, reflection and insight to see through ignorance and recognize the true self. It is closely tied to the Upanishads and to Advaita teachers such as Shankara. A student on this path might ask, again and again, who am I, and set aside every answer that names only the body or the mind.

The path of devotion is *bhakti yoga*: love and surrender to a personal God. Bhakti movements spread across India from about the 6th century CE onward, carried by poet-saints who sang in everyday languages instead of Sanskrit. The 16th-century poet Mirabai, a devotee of Krishna, is still sung today. Many scholars describe bhakti as the most widely practiced path today. The path of action is *karma yoga*: doing one's duty without selfish attachment to results, a teaching at the heart of the Bhagavad Gita.

The path of meditation is often called raja yoga, the royal path. It trains the body, breath and mind to reach deep stillness. It draws on the Yoga Sutras attributed to Patanjali. Many Hindus see these paths as suited to different temperaments, and most mix them. The Gita itself teaches all of them.

words.d: joining or discipline; in Hindu thought, a path or practice that leads toward union with the divine or liberation
the path of knowledge, seeking liberation through insight into the true self
the path of devotion, seeking liberation through love for a personal God
the path of action, doing one's duty without attachment to the results

look.title: Match the Path
look.text: Anjali volunteers at a food pantry every Saturday and never posts about it. Dev reads the Upanishads with a study group and keeps a journal of questions about the self. Meera joins a temple choir that sings to Krishna for hours. Arun practices breathing exercises and silent meditation at dawn.
look.prompt: Name the path each person is following, and explain one clue from the text for each.

check.q: What is bhakti yoga?
choices: The path of loving devotion to a personal God
The path of study and insight
The path of breath control and stretching
The path of wealth and success
check.why: Bhakti is devotion. Jnana is knowledge, and artha, not a yoga, is the goal of wealth.

check.q: Which path does the Bhagavad Gita describe as doing one's duty without selfish attachment to results?
choices: Jnana yoga
Raja yoga
Karma yoga
Hatha yoga
check.why: Karma yoga is selfless action, a central teaching of the Bhagavad Gita.

check.q: Why did bhakti poet-saints such as Mirabai reach so many people?
choices: They wrote only for priests
They sang in everyday languages rather than only in Sanskrit
They rejected all worship of deities
They lived before the Vedas
check.why: Bhakti poets sang in the languages people spoke, making devotion open to everyone.

lessons.title: Puja at Home and in the Temple
lessons.mainIdea: Puja is Hindu worship through offerings of light, flowers, food and prayer, performed at home shrines and in temples.
reading: Early in the morning, a woman in a Chicago suburb bathes, then stands before a small shrine in her kitchen. She lights a lamp and a stick of incense. She offers a flower and a little rice to an image of Ganesha, and quietly recites a prayer. This takes five minutes. It is *puja*, worship through offerings, and in many Hindu homes it happens every day.

In a temple, puja is larger. A priest bathes, dresses and adorns the *murti*, the sacred image of the deity. Many Hindus believe the deity is truly present in the murti once it has been consecrated. During arati, the priest waves a lamp in circles before the image while worshipers sing. Food offered to the deity is then shared among worshipers as *prasad*, a blessed gift. Worshipers remove their shoes before entering, as a sign of respect.

The Bhagavad Gita offers a line many Hindus quote about puja: Krishna says that whoever offers him even a leaf, a flower, a fruit or water with devotion, he accepts it. The point is the love behind the offering, not its cost. This helps explain why puja can be simple or grand.

Hindu temples are called mandirs. The Chicago area has many, including the Hindu Temple of Greater Chicago in Lemont and the Sri Venkateswara Swami Temple in Aurora. For many families in the United States, the temple is also a community center with language classes, dance lessons and festival meals.

words.d: Hindu worship through offerings such as light, flowers, food and prayer
a consecrated sacred image of a deity, in which many Hindus believe the deity is present
food first offered to a deity and then shared among worshipers as a blessing
a Hindu temple

look.title: A Leaf, a Flower, a Fruit
look.text: Whoever offers me with devotion a leaf, a flower, a fruit or a little water, that offering of love from a pure heart I accept. Whatever you do, whatever you eat, whatever you offer or give, do it as an offering to me.

choices: Food offered to a deity and then shared with worshipers as a blessing
The lamp waved during arati
The stone steps along a river
A hymn from the Rig Veda
check.why: Prasad is blessed food returned to worshipers after it is offered to the deity.

check.q: What is a murti?
choices: A school for learning Sanskrit
A consecrated image in which many Hindus believe the deity is present
A kind of festival sweet
A book of Hindu law
check.why: A murti is the sacred image of a deity in a home or temple shrine.

check.q: According to Bhagavad Gita 9.26, what matters most in an offering?
choices: Its price
That a priest performs it
That it is made in Sanskrit
The devotion behind it
check.why: Krishna says he accepts even a leaf or water offered with devotion, so love matters more than cost.

lessons.title: Diwali and Holi
lessons.mainIdea: Diwali, the festival of lights, and Holi, the spring festival of colors, are among the most widely celebrated Hindu holidays, each with several stories behind it.
reading: Hindu festivals follow a lunar calendar, so their dates on the Western calendar shift each year. *Diwali* usually falls in October or November, on the new moon of the month of Kartik. It lasts about five days. Families clean their homes, light rows of diyas, set off fireworks, share sweets and wear new clothes. Many worship Lakshmi, goddess of good fortune, and many business owners begin a new account book.

Diwali carries several stories. In northern India, many remember Rama's return to Ayodhya after his exile and his victory over the demon king Ravana. In parts of South India, many recall Krishna's defeat of the demon Narakasura. The shared theme is light overcoming darkness and good overcoming evil. Jains observe Diwali as the day their teacher Mahavira reached liberation, and Sikhs celebrate Bandi Chhor Divas on the same days.

*Holi* comes in early spring, on the full moon of the month of Phalguna. On the night before, many communities light bonfires recalling the story of Prahlad, a young devotee of Vishnu saved from the fire, while his wicked aunt Holika burned. The next morning, people throw colored powder and water at each other in the streets. Many connect the colors to Krishna's playful youth.

For a day, Holi loosens social rules. Old and young, rich and poor, may all end up covered in pink and green. In Chicago, Holi gatherings at temples, parks and universities often welcome people of any background, and many non-Hindu students join in the colors.

words.d: the Hindu festival of lights in autumn, celebrating the victory of light over darkness
the Hindu spring festival of colors, marked by bonfires and throwing colored powder
a small clay oil lamp lit at Diwali and in worship
a calendar based on the phases of the moon, so festival dates shift on the Western calendar

look.title: One Festival, Several Stories
look.text: A class survey asks five students why their families light lamps at Diwali. Answers: to welcome Lakshmi; to remember Rama coming home to Ayodhya; to celebrate Krishna defeating Narakasura; to honor Mahavira's liberation, from a Jain student; and to mark Bandi Chhor Divas, from a Sikh student.
look.prompt: Is one of these answers the correct one? Explain how a scholar of religion would describe a festival with several meanings.

check.q: Why do the dates of Diwali and Holi change on the Western calendar each year?
choices: Because they follow a Hindu lunar calendar
Because each temple picks its own date
Because the Indian government moves them
Because they depend on the weather
check.why: Hindu festivals follow a lunar calendar, so their dates shift relative to the solar Western calendar.

check.q: Which story is connected to the bonfires the night before Holi?
choices: Rama's return to Ayodhya
Prahlad, a devotee of Vishnu, saved from the fire while Holika burned
Krishna teaching Arjuna on the battlefield
Shiva dancing in a ring of flames
check.why: Holi bonfires recall Prahlad's rescue and Holika's burning. Rama's return is connected to Diwali.

lessons.title: Caste: History and Reform
lessons.mainIdea: Caste is a system of inherited social groups in South Asia; Hindus and reformers have long debated it, and India's Constitution, in force from 1950, outlawed untouchability.
reading: Caste is one of the most debated subjects in the study of Hinduism, and it should be described carefully. Ancient Hindu texts describe four varnas, or classes (each one a *varna*): Brahmins, priests and teachers; Kshatriyas, rulers and warriors; Vaishyas, merchants and farmers; and Shudras, laborers and servants. One Rig Veda hymn pictures these classes coming from different parts of a cosmic being. In practice, daily life was organized by thousands of smaller birth groups, each called a *jati*, often tied to an occupation and a region.

Over centuries, some groups were placed outside the varnas and treated as untouchable. They faced exclusion from temples, wells and schools. Many members of these communities today use the name *Dalit*, meaning broken or oppressed, as a name of dignity and protest. Caste also affected other religious communities in South Asia, not only Hindus.

Criticism of caste is old. Many bhakti poet-saints taught that God welcomes every devotee, whatever their birth. In the 19th and 20th centuries, reformers pushed harder. Gandhi campaigned against untouchability. B. R. Ambedkar, a Dalit lawyer and scholar, fought caste discrimination, chaired the committee that drafted India's Constitution, and in 1956 converted to Buddhism with a large number of followers. The Constitution, which took effect in 1950, abolished untouchability and banned caste discrimination.

Today caste is still a live issue. Many Hindus say it is a social custom, not a core religious teaching, and point to the Upanishads' claim that the same atman lives in every being. Others argue that religious texts helped support the system. Caste discrimination has also become a public issue in some American workplaces and universities. A fair student of religion describes both the history and the reform.

words.d: one of the four broad classes described in ancient Hindu texts
a birth group in the caste system, often linked to an occupation and region; there are thousands
a name of dignity chosen by many people from communities once treated as untouchable

look.title: Text and Society
look.text: Text 1: The Upanishads teach that the same atman, the true self, lives in every being. Text 2: A Rig Veda hymn describes the four varnas coming from the mouth, arms, thighs and feet of a cosmic being. Reformer: Ambedkar argued that the caste system must be abolished, and he left Hinduism in 1956.
look.prompt: How might a Hindu reformer use Text 1 against caste? How might a critic use Text 2? Why did Ambedkar's response differ from Gandhi's?

It left the question to each temple

review.q: Which statement best describes Hinduism as scholars study it?
choices: A single church founded in 1500 BCE
A family of related traditions with no single founder, book or central authority
A religion that teaches belief in one God only, with no images
A tradition practiced only in India
review.why: Hinduism is a family of traditions with shared ideas and stories but no founder or central authority.

review.q: In the Upanishads, how are Brahman and atman related?
choices: Brahman is the self and atman is a festival
Atman is a god of fire and Brahman is a priest
They are two names for the four Vedas
Many passages teach that the deepest self, atman, is one with the ultimate reality, Brahman
review.why: The Upanishads, as in the salt-and-water story, teach that atman and Brahman are at bottom the same.

review.q: Which sequence correctly links these ideas?
choices: Karma shapes rebirth in samsara, and moksha is release from samsara
Moksha causes karma, which ends dharma
Samsara is release from karma
Dharma is the cycle of rebirth, and karma is liberation
review.why: Karma, the result of actions, shapes rebirth within samsara; moksha is liberation from that cycle.

review.q: A Hindu offers a flower to Krishna each morning and sings his name at night. Which path is this?
choices: Jnana yoga
Raja yoga
Bhakti yoga
Artha
review.why: Loving devotion to a personal God such as Krishna is bhakti yoga.

review.q: Which deity is honored by nearly all Hindus as the remover of obstacles?
choices: Ganesha
Brahma
Indra
Kali
review.why: Ganesha, the elephant-headed son of Shiva and Parvati, is the remover of obstacles.

review.q: What do Shaivas, Vaishnavas and Shaktas each see as supreme?
choices: Ganesha, Rama and Agni
Shiva, Vishnu and the Goddess Devi
Brahma, Shiva and Lakshmi
The Vedas, the Gita and the Puranas

review.q: Why do Jains and Sikhs also celebrate on the days of Diwali?
choices: Because they worship Lakshmi above all
Because they are forms of Hinduism
Because Rama was their founder
Because the days mark Mahavira's liberation for Jains and Bandi Chhor Divas for Sikhs
review.why: Jains and Sikhs have their own reasons for marking these days, which shows festivals can carry several meanings.

review.q: Which of these texts is shruti?
choices: The Mahabharata
The Ramayana
The Rig Veda
A Puranic story of Ganesha
review.why: The Vedas are shruti, what is heard. The epics and Puranas are smriti, what is remembered.
